label: Your home parish
blurb: Familiar pews, a pastor who knew you before, and a summer of being watched by people who remember you as a boy.
outcome: You are fed, photographed, and asked to say grace at every table. The pastor lets you do more than he should. You come back rested and a little embarrassed by how easy it was.

label: A hard parish
blurb: Somewhere nobody asked for: a neighborhood with more funerals than baptisms, a pastor alone, a rectory with one working shower.
outcome: You learn what a parish looks like when it is losing. You bury people whose names you never learned to pronounce and you sit with a pastor who has stopped expecting help. The formation faculty notice that you asked for it.

label: Hospital chaplaincy
blurb: A unit of clinical pastoral education: the wards, the night pager, the families in the hallway.
outcome: You sit with the dying and with people who are angry at God and at you. You learn to say nothing well. The supervisor's evaluation is blunt and, in places, correct.

label: A mission abroad
blurb: Eight weeks somewhere hot with the diocese's sister mission: a school, a clinic, Mass under a tin roof.
outcome: You come back thinner, with a tan and a set of opinions about American parishes that you will have to learn to keep to yourself. Your Spanish is better. So is your prayer.

label: A chancery internship
blurb: Filing, driving, sitting outside meetings. Seeing how the diocese is actually run.
outcome: You learn who signs what and who decides before the signing. Two officials remember your name. One of them is worth remembering back.

label: A summer in Rome
blurb: Italian classes, the Roman churches, and a chance to be seen by the people who notice.
outcome: You learn enough Italian to be embarrassed by it and enough about Rome to want to go back. The rector hears that you did well. So does someone at the Congregation, though you will not know it for years.

label: Spanish immersion
blurb: A language school in Mexico or Guatemala, host family included, for men the diocese needs to be bilingual.
outcome: By August you can hear confessions in Spanish badly and preach in it worse, which is more than most of the presbyterate. The vocation director writes it down.

label: A regular parish
blurb: A suburban parish with a school, three Masses on Sunday, and a pastor who will let you do as much as you ask for. The ordinary summer, which is most of the priesthood.
outcome: You learn the sacristy, the sick list, the Knights, the parish picnic, and the pastor's way of doing things, which is not the seminary's. Nothing happens that anyone will write down. You come back knowing what the job is on a Tuesday, which the seminary cannot teach.

label: A Spanish-speaking parish
blurb: A parish where the noon Mass is in Spanish and the eight o'clock is the one that is thin. Your Spanish, such as it is, will be used from the first Sunday.
outcome: You baptize in Spanish by July, badly, and hear your first quinceañera homily criticized by a grandmother in a language you half follow. The parish is generous with a man who tries. By August the vocation director has heard where you spent the summer, and it goes in the file under the heading the diocese is shortest in.

label: The Polish parish
blurb: A parish that was Poland once and is still Polish at the eleven o'clock: the older people, the language, a pastor who came from Kraków thirty years ago and has not gone back.
outcome: You learn to say the responses in Polish and the pastor teaches you, with some contempt, to sing. The parish is old and knows it. In August a widow tells you that you would have made a good Polish priest, which is meant as a high compliment and received as one.

label: The Vietnamese parish
blurb: A parish built by refugees and run by their sons: a Mass in Vietnamese that fills, a youth group of two hundred, and a pastor who was a boat person and does not speak of it.
outcome: You learn the feasts, the food, the way the community keeps its priests, and the shape of a parish in which every family is a story. The pastor tells you, at the end, that you listened, which from him is the summer's whole grade.

label: A Black Catholic parish
blurb: A parish with a gospel choir, a two-hour Mass, and a history older than the diocese's: the people who stayed when the neighborhood changed and the ones who came back for it.
outcome: You learn to preach to a congregation that answers, which changes how you preach. The pastor, who has buried more parishioners than he has baptized, tells you the parish's history in pieces over the summer, and by August you know why the choir sings what it sings. It is not a summer the file has a heading for. It is one you will not forget.

label: Catholic Charities
blurb: A summer in the diocese's social arm: the food pantry, the immigration office, the shelter, and a staff of lay professionals who will watch to see whether a seminarian is any use.
outcome: You are some use. You learn what the diocese does for people who will never come to Mass, and what it costs, and who pays. The director writes to the vocation director that you can be given a desk and left. It is a sentence the chancery reads with interest.

label: The Newman Center
blurb: The Catholic center at the state university: a summer session of a few hundred students, a chaplain who is tired, and a chapel that fills at nine at night.
outcome: You run the Tuesday supper and preach the nine o'clock and are asked, by a twenty-year-old, every question you ever asked at twenty. Two of them will write to you in the autumn. The chaplain says, at the end, that the students liked you, and that this is not always a good sign, and that in your case it is.

label: The shrine
blurb: The diocese's shrine in its busy season: pilgrims by the busload, confessions all day in four languages, a rector who runs it like a railway.
outcome: You hear confessions you cannot yet absolve and sit beside the priest who can, and learn what people carry to a shrine. The rector, who has seen a hundred seminarians, says that you did not get in the way, which is his highest praise, and writes it down.

label: A rural mission circuit
blurb: Three churches and a chapel, ninety miles of road between them, one priest, and a summer of driving to say Mass for eleven people who would otherwise have none.
outcome: You learn the roads, the names, the farms, and the particular loneliness of a priest who is the only one for sixty miles. The pastor, who has been there twenty years, says that most seminarians ask to leave by July and that you did not. The chancery hears it. It is the summer that the file under 'shortage' likes best.

label: The diocesan media office
blurb: The paper, the radio hour, the bishop's video messages: a summer writing what the diocese says about itself, under an editor who used to work for a real newspaper.
outcome: You learn to write a sentence the bishop can say and to cut the ones he cannot, and something about how a diocese looks from the outside. The editor tells the chancery that you can write, which is rarer than the chancery would like. Your name is on three things by August.

label: Storm season with the diocese
blurb: The diocese's disaster office in the months when the weather comes: shelters in parish halls, generators, the phone tree, and a bishop who wants to be seen in waders.
outcome: One storm comes, or two, and you learn what a parish hall is for and how the diocese moves when it must. You spend a week in a shelter with three hundred people and a deacon who runs it like a ship. The chancery remembers the men who were there.

label: The cathedral on Fifth Avenue
blurb: A summer as the least of the cathedral's staff: tourists, the noon Mass with six hundred strangers, the cardinal's masters of ceremonies, and a sacristy that has seen everything.
outcome: You learn a liturgy done at scale and the particular humility of being the fourth man in a procession the cameras are on. The rector of the cathedral, who knows every priest of the archdiocese, learns your name, and so, at one Mass, does the cardinal, briefly.

label: A Bronx parish
blurb: A parish in the Bronx with four Masses in three languages, a school that is the neighborhood's only quiet building, and a pastor who has not taken a day off since the nineties.
outcome: You take the pastor's Tuesday and he does not know what to do with it. You learn the building, the block, the bodega, the funeral home, and the way a parish holds a neighborhood together with string. The people are glad of you in the way people are glad of anyone who stays.

label: Two churches, one pastor, on the South Side
blurb: A merged parish: two churches a mile apart, one closing, a pastor who drives between them on Sunday and is hated in both for different reasons.
outcome: You learn what consolidation costs the people it is done to, and what it costs the man who does it. You say the last Mass in one of the churches in August, as deacon of nothing, and the people leave the pews as if leaving a wake. The chancery notes that you saw it through.

label: The county jail chaplaincy
blurb: A summer at the county jail with the archdiocese's chaplains: Mass on the tiers, a Bible study in a room with no windows, and men who can tell in a minute whether you are afraid.
outcome: You are afraid for a week and then you are not, and the chaplain notices the day it changes. You learn the jail, its rules, its two kinds of quiet. One man asks you to write to his mother and you do. The archdiocese keeps a list of priests who will go inside, and your name is on it before you are ordained.

label: Skid Row
blurb: The archdiocese's mission on Skid Row: a chapel, a clinic, a shower line, and a priest who has been there since the eighties and does not want a seminarian, and takes one every summer.
outcome: You learn names first, because he insists, and the rest after. By August you can walk the block and be greeted. You have seen what the city does with the people it does not want, and what the Church does, which is less than it should and more than anyone else. The priest tells the vocation director you can come back.

label: A Filipino parish in the Valley
blurb: A parish in the San Fernando Valley that is Filipino at every Mass: the Santo Niño, the simbang gabi remembered in July, a hundred nurses, and a pastor who was ordained in Manila.
outcome: You are fed until you cannot stand and taught the devotions one by one. The parish's warmth is a formation of its own. The pastor, who sends men to the seminary every few years, says you understood the people, which he does not say of every seminarian the archdiocese sends him.

label: A parish on the ring, half built
blurb: A parish founded four years ago on the highway ring, saying Mass in a gym while the church goes up, with two thousand families and a pastor who is also the general contractor.
outcome: You learn a parish that is being invented: the first Knights council, the first Spanish Mass, the first funeral in a gym. The pastor hands you the youth group and the building committee minutes on the same day. The diocese, which is building faster than it can staff, notes that you did not drown.

label: The ship channel parish
blurb: A parish by the refineries on the ship channel: shift workers, a Mass at six in the morning for the night shift, an air that smells of the plants, and a pastor who buries a man from the refineries every month.
outcome: You learn the plants' shifts and the parish's, and the way a town lives with what it breathes. A man dies at the plant in July and the funeral is the largest you have seen. The pastor says the parish will remember that you were there, and it will.

label: The bishops' conference offices
blurb: A summer as an intern at the bishops' conference: the committees, the documents, the staff who have outlasted six presidents, and the way the Church in America talks to itself.
outcome: You learn how a statement is written, by whom, and how many drafts it takes to say nothing. You also learn that the people in the building know every bishop in the country and what he is like. One of them remembers your name. It is a small thing and it is how careers in that building begin.

label: Southern Maryland, the oldest parishes
blurb: The parishes in Southern Maryland founded before the Republic: tobacco country, a church from 1690, families who have been Catholic here for eleven generations and know it.
outcome: You learn a Catholicism older than the country and quieter than the city's: the cemeteries, the Jesuit fields, the old families' pews. The pastor, who is one of the old families, tells you the history over eight weeks of suppers. It is a summer the chancery does not notice and you will.

label: Closing a parish
blurb: A parish the archdiocese has decided to close, with a pastor who has been told to close it by September and a people who have been told nothing they believe.
outcome: You are there for the last Masses, the packing of the sacristy, the meeting in the hall where a woman of eighty asks the pastor where she is supposed to be buried. You learn what the diocese asks of a priest when it asks the worst thing. The chancery, which sent you, remembers that you went.

label: The Main Line
blurb: A parish on the Main Line: old money, a school with a waiting list, a pastor who dines with the families that fund the seminary, and a summer of being looked over.
outcome: You learn how the archdiocese's money thinks, and that its families are Catholic in a way that is both deeper and more particular than you had assumed. Two of them ask the pastor about you. The pastor, who is careful, says only good things, and you understand that he was asked.

label: The Cape in season
blurb: A parish on Cape Cod in its summer: a church that seats four hundred and holds eight hundred in July, five Masses on Sunday, and a pastor who counts the weeks until Labor Day.
outcome: You say Mass for people who will never come back and hear confessions from people who have not been in years and came because they were on vacation. The pastor says that the Cape is a mission field with parking, and by August you understand him.

label: The Brazilian parish
blurb: A parish in a mill town that has become Brazilian in twenty years: Mass in Portuguese, a choir with drums, a pastor from Minas Gerais, and an older Irish remnant that comes to the eight.
outcome: You learn to say the responses in Portuguese and to be laughed at kindly. The parish's two halves are a lesson in what a diocese is becoming and what it was. The pastor says you were good with the old people and the young ones both, which is the whole trick.

label: The Tenderloin
blurb: A parish in the Tenderloin: a soup line, a needle on the church steps most mornings, a Mass for forty, and a pastor who has been there long enough to be part of the block.
outcome: You learn to open the church in the morning and what you will find there, and to say Mass for people who came in for the quiet. The pastor teaches you the block's names. It is a summer that costs something and pays in a currency the file does not record.

label: The Chinese mission
blurb: The archdiocese's Chinese mission: Mass in Cantonese, a school that is the community's pride, and a pastor who was ordained in Hong Kong and has opinions about Rome.
outcome: You learn the mission's history, from the earthquake forward, and the community's way of holding its priests close. You are useless in Cantonese and useful at the school, and the pastor, who is exact, says so in that order to the vocation director.

label: Little Haiti
blurb: A parish in Little Haiti: Mass in Creole, a choir that shakes the building, a pastor from Port-au-Prince, and a people who have buried more than any parish should.
outcome: You learn a Creole Mass by ear and the parish's grief and joy, which come together. The pastor, who has seen the archdiocese send him seminarians who counted the days, says you did not count. It reaches the vocation director in those words.

label: The Keys, the parish at the end of the road
blurb: A parish at the far end of the Keys: tourists, fishermen, a chapel by the water, and one priest for a hundred miles of highway.
outcome: You learn the priest's circuit, the hurricane plan, and the loneliness of a parish that the mainland forgets. You say Mass on a dock once. The priest, who is not sent seminarians often, writes a letter about you that the chancery did not expect and files.

label: A river parish in French Louisiana
blurb: A parish on the river below the city: French names on every grave, a church from the 1840s, crawfish after Mass, and a pastor who is a cousin of half the parish.
outcome: You learn the river, the families, and a Catholicism that has been here longer than the state. The pastor takes you to every supper he is invited to, which is all of them. By August you can tell the families apart, which the parish regards as the beginning of wisdom.

label: The parish in the Quarter
blurb: A parish in the French Quarter: tourists at every Mass, a homeless man in the vestibule who has been there longer than the pastor, weddings on Saturdays and the city's noise on the steps.
outcome: You learn a parish that belongs to everyone and no one, and how to preach to a congregation that will not be there next week. The pastor, who is famous in a small way, teaches you what he knows about that. The archdiocese, which watches the Quarter, sees you in it.
